lead: A wing web is made thin to save weight, and a thin plate in shear buckles long before the beam fails. The wrinkled web cannot carry more than its buckling stress, so the extra shear travels as a diagonal tension band stretched between the booms. Wagner's theory turns that picture into two numbers: the diagonal tension factor k, which splits the applied shear between web and band, and the angle α of the band. It is the standard way to size spar webs, fuselage shear webs and any beam allowed to buckle below limit load.
prereq: You need: the boom–panel model and the shear flow q = S/d from 5.6, the shear flow idea itself from 5.1, and plate shear buckling from Unit 6, Plates, Buckling and Composite Structures.

blocks.text: A thin web carries shear as τ_av = S/(t d): S is the applied shear in N, t the web thickness in mm, d the web depth between boom centroids in mm. In the boom–panel model of 5.6 this is the shear flow q = S/d, in N/mm.

This holds only while the web stays flat. A plate in shear buckles at a critical stress τ_cr; Unit 6 gives the plate coefficients for a given panel shape. The web then wrinkles along one diagonal, close to 45° to the flanges, because pure shear has its principal tension on that diagonal.
Buckling is not failure. The wrinkled web keeps carrying shear but cannot climb much above τ_cr. The surplus travels as a diagonal tension band, which hands the load to the booms.

blocks.where: τ_av is the nominal (pre-buckling) average shear stress in the web in N/mm²; S is the applied shear force in N; t is the web thickness in mm; d is the web depth between boom centroids in mm.

sections.h3: The diagonal tension band and the factor k

blocks.text: After buckling the web acts like diagonal straps in tension: the diagonal tension field, inclined at angle α to the booms. Wagner's theory describes it with one number, the diagonal tension factor k.
k = 1 − τ_cr / τ_av = (S − τ_cr · t · d) / S
blocks.where: k is the diagonal tension factor, a pure number between 0 and 1; τ_av = S/(t d) is the nominal web shear stress in N/mm²; τ_cr is the shear buckling stress of the web in N/mm².

blocks.text: The web stress is stuck at τ_cr, so the web carries S_w = τ_cr t d = (1 − k) S. The band carries the rest, ΔS = k S. A web that never buckles has k = 0: a shear-resistant web beam. A web with no shear capacity has k = 1: complete diagonal tension.

head: k
How the shear travels
rows: Web carries all of it; shear-resistant web beam
Web at τ_cr, band carries the surplus
Web carries nothing; complete diagonal tension

blocks.text: The band supplies ΔS through its tension σ_t: ΔS = σ_t t d sinα cosα. Since sinα cosα = ½ sin 2α, the product peaks at 0.5 at α = 45°, so a 45° band needs the least tension.
σ_t = ΔS / (t · d · sin α · cos α)
blocks.where: σ_t is the diagonal tension stress in the web in N/mm²; ΔS = k S is the shear carried by the band in N; α is the angle of the band to the booms in degrees; t and d are in mm.

blocks.text: Statics does not fix α. Compatibility between boom stretching and web stretching does: stiff booms hold the band near 45°, softer booms let it rotate towards the flange direction. Most aircraft webs sit between 30° and 45°.

sections.h3: Boom loads and the Wagner beam

blocks.text: The band is anchored to the booms. Over one bay of length L between ribs, each boom gains axial force P = ΔS L/d.
P = ΔS · L / d = k · S · L / d
blocks.where: P is the axial force added to one boom over the bay in N; L is the rib spacing (bay length) in mm; d is the web depth in mm; ΔS = k S is the band shear in N.

blocks.text: The total boom force still rises at S/d per unit length, because global equilibrium does not care how the shear is carried. Only the route changes: the web delivers (1 − k) S/d and the band k S/d. Add them once, never twice.

A beam of booms plus a web in diagonal tension is a Wagner beam; some syllabi call the method tension field theory. Wing and fuselage webs are often made thinner than the buckling limit on purpose: the booms and stringers are there anyway and can absorb the tension. Ribs and bulkheads anchor the field, and their spacing L fixes the boom force.
If the web stays below τ_cr at limit load, ignore all of this: use the shear flow of 5.2 and 5.3 and set k = 0.

spec.title: Wagner beam: from applied shear to boom load
spec.aria: A downward flow chart: applied shear of 80 kN buckles the web at 60 N/mm², a diagonal tension band forms at 45 degrees, and the shear splits into 45 kN of web shear and 52.5 kN of boom axial load per bay.

examples.question: A thin-webbed beam has a web 500 mm deep and 1.5 mm thick, and booms of area 300 mm² each. It carries 80 kN. The web buckles at τ_cr = 60 N/mm², the band runs at α = 45°, and ribs anchor it every 750 mm. Find (a) the nominal web shear stress, (b) k, (c) the shear split, (d) σ_t, (e) the axial force added to each boom over one bay, and the boom stress.
steps: Nominal web shear stress: τ_av = 80 000 N / (1.5 mm × 500 mm) = 106.7 N/mm²; the real web is capped at 60 N/mm².
Web share: S_w = 60 N/mm² × 1.5 mm × 500 mm = 45 000 N = 45 kN.
Band share: ΔS = 80 − 45 = 35 kN. Diagonal tension factor: k = 35/80 = 0.4375.
examples.answer: k = 0.4375; web 45 kN, band 35 kN; σ_t = 93.3 N/mm²; each boom gains 52.5 kN over 750 mm, giving 175 N/mm².
examples.check:
import math
d = 500.0
t = 1.5
A = 300.0
S = 80000.0
tau_cr = 60.0
L = 750.0
alpha = math.radians(45.0)
tau_av = S / (t * d)
S_web = tau_cr * t * d
dS = S - S_web
k = dS / S
sigma_t = dS / (t * d * math.sin(alpha) * math.cos(alpha))
P = dS * L / d
sigma_b = P / A
print(round(tau_av, 1))
print(round(S_web / 1000.0, 1))
print(round(dS / 1000.0, 1))
print(round(k, 4))
print(round(sigma_t, 1))
print(round(P / 1000.0, 1))
print(round(sigma_b, 1))

traps: Using τ = S/(t d) as the web stress after buckling. The web stress stays at τ_cr; that equation only gives the nominal value.
Saying the web 'fails' at τ_cr. It wrinkles, keeps carrying about τ_cr, and the diagonal tension band restores the strength.
Swapping shares: the web carries (1 − k)S and the band kS, so k = 0.44 means the band takes 44 per cent, not the web.
Dropping the sin α cos α product or its ½ from the double-angle form. At 45° the product is 0.5, not 1, and dropping it halves σ_t (93.3 N/mm² becomes 46.7 N/mm²), an unsafe underestimate.
Adding the diagonal tension boom force on top of the full S/d gradient. Global equilibrium still fixes the total gradient at S/d; the Wagner term only splits it.

quiz.q: Define the diagonal tension factor k and state its range.
quiz.a: k = 1 − τ_cr/τ_av = (S − τ_cr t d)/S, with τ_av = S/(t d). It lies between 0 and 1: 0 for a shear-resistant web, 1 for complete diagonal tension.

quiz.q: What is a shear-resistant web beam?
quiz.a: A beam whose web is thick enough to carry the whole shear without buckling, so q = S/d and k = 0.

quiz.q: Why do the web wrinkles run at about 45° to the flanges?
quiz.a: Pure shear has principal tension and compression on the 45° diagonals. The web buckles against the compression diagonal, so the wrinkles follow the tension diagonal.

quiz.q: Explain why the beam does not collapse when its web buckles.
quiz.a: The buckled web still carries about τ_cr, and the diagonal tension band carries the surplus shear into the booms. Stiffness falls; strength and load path remain.

quiz.q: A web 400 mm deep and 1.2 mm thick carries 60 kN and buckles at τ_cr = 50 N/mm². Find the nominal web stress, the web share of the shear, and k.
For the worked example (ΔS = 35 kN, t = 1.5 mm, d = 500 mm), repeat the diagonal tension stress for α = 30°.
quiz.a: sin 30° cos 30° = 0.4330. σ_t = 35 000/(1.5 × 500 × 0.4330) = 35 000/324.8 = 107.8 N/mm². A smaller angle needs higher band stress.

quiz.q: The same 80 kN beam keeps d, t and booms, but τ_cr drops from 60 to 30 N/mm². Discuss the load path and the booms.
quiz.a: S_w = 30 × 1.5 × 500 = 22.5 kN, so ΔS = 57.5 kN and k = 0.72. Band stress rises to 57 500/375 = 153.3 N/mm², and each boom gains 57 500 × 750/500 = 86.3 kN per bay. The booms now carry most of the shear, and the ribs anchor a stronger field.

beyond: Not for the exam. Post-buckled shear webs are normal in transport aircraft spars, and the tension field idea reappears in stiffened panels: the skin buckles between stringers, and the stringers take the diagonal pull. Research couples Wagner's statics with imperfection-sensitive finite element models, because real webs buckle below the ideal plate value. Composite webs behave differently: they cannot yield and may split along the band. Search for diagonal tension field, Wagner beam, post-buckled shear web, and semi-tension field design.
